segments.text: Pure Point Uranium Group Inc CEO Chris
Frostad talked with Proactive about the
company's latest uranium exploration
progress at its Dorado project in northern
Saskatchewan, as well as the broader
process behind making and advancing a
discovery.
Frostad explained that Pure Point Uranium
Group operates in one of the world's most
prolific uranium regions and works
alongside major partners including Cameco,
Orano, and IsoEnergy.
The discussion focused on the company's
recent discovery at the Dorado project,
specifically within the Nova zone, where
initial drilling intersected high-grade
uranium mineralization.
Proactive.
Welcome back inside our Proactive
newsroom. Joining me now is Chris Frostad,
CEO of Pure Point Uranium Group.
Chris, good to see you. How are you?
Good to be here. I'm doing really well
right now. We're getting out of the
wintertime, and things are looking a
little sunnier here in Toronto.
For those not familiar, give us some
background on the company.
Pure Point is a uranium exploration
company operating in northern
Saskatchewan, where all of Canada's
uranium comes from.
We work with significant partners
including Cameco, Orano, and IsoEnergy.
Most recently, we've been following up on
our Dorado project, a joint venture with
IsoEnergy.
You've made a discovery there. What does
that mean in practice?
Most exploration drilling in northern
Saskatchewan finds no uranium.
When you do find something meaningful that
can be tied to a broader system, it's
considered a discovery and needs
follow-up.
What happens next after a discovery?
The real work happens after the fact. You
need to determine if the result is
repeatable. Rather than drilling randomly,
you expand around the initial hole,
above, below, and laterally to better
understand the mineralization.
How important is technology in this
process?
It's critical.
Uranium is invisible to geophysics, so we
look for indirect indicators like rock
types and structures. Once drilling
begins, we integrate that data with
geophysics to understand what controls the
mineralization.
Is that where modeling comes in?
Exactly. You build a model to understand
direction and controls.
Then you can step out, sometimes hundreds
of meters, to see if mineralization
continues and refine your targeting.
How does this apply to Dorado?
We made a discovery at the Nova zone,
hitting high-grade uranium in a specific
area. We drilled four holes and identified
a direction of continuity. Now we're
following up with additional drilling,
including step outs, to better understand
the system and plan the next phase.
